newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan investment in China seen cooling - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan investment in China seen cooling - analysts.

text.p: Taipei's plan to freeze economic initiatives with rival China in retaliation against Beijing's successful courtship of South Africa will cool private investment to the mainland in the near future, analysts said.

But they added companies that had already poured money into China would not abandon their projects just to comply with government policy, and pure market incentives ultimately would draw investors back to China.

In a policy shift triggered by South Africa's announcement to sever diplomatic ties with Taipei and recognise Beijing in 1997, Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council said on Friday it would not launch further steps to boost economic links with China.

"The (council's) announcement will deter new investors from entering the China market knowing that the government is not fully behind them," said Joe Chiou, securities analyst for Taiwan Securities Investment.
"But many companies already have huge projects in and even shifted their entire operation focus to China, and they are not going to drop everything just because the government is angry," Chiou said.

Some 25,000 Taiwan businesses have poured over US$20 billion into the Chinese mainland, making Taiwan one of the leading overseas investors in China -- and China one of Taiwan's most important markets.
But recently Taiwan's government has warned that the island's economy must not become overdependent on the mainland, and several major firms have called off China projects in apparent compliance.

The state monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp said on Tuesday it had stalled a plan for joint oil exploration with China, adding: "We are a state company and we have to comply with the government's policy."
State firms have not been the only ones answering the government's admonition.
Food giant President Enterprises in September abandoned a plan to build a US$100 million power plant in China.

In August, Formosa Plastic Group announced it was calling off a deal to build what would have been the biggest Taiwan project in China to date -- a US$3 billion power plant project in coastal Fujian province.

"The bigger firms with more high-profile projects will be the ones affected the most if the government does not want to encourage investment (in China)," said Allen Huang, a senior manager at National Securities.
But Huang added that any politically driven boycott would not prevail and market factors eventually would lure enterprises back to China.

"There is a saying in Chinese that businessmen do not belong to any country. Basically, investors will go where there is money to be made, and no one doubts that China has huge opportunities," Huang said.
George Hou, a fund manager for Jardine Fleming, said even the government would soften its stance after the clamour over Pretoria's fallout dies down.
"When a country abandons Taiwan for China, it is natural for the government to act tough and put up a short-term defiance. But at the end things will return to where they started," Hou said.

Taiwan and China have been rivals since a civil war divided them in 1949. Although Taiwan began allowing indirect trade to China with the easing of cross-strait tensions in the 1980s, it is concerned about becoming political vulnerable if China ties up too much of its economy.
